key_test: Recognise the combined effect of poor drainage, a visibly soft surface, water in wheel tracks, a heavy machinery load, recent rainfall and further forecast rainfall.
Refuse to assess tractor access without information about field condition, drainage, recent weather, forecast weather and machinery load.
Return a lower risk assessment when direct inspection finds firm ground with no standing water while soil, weather and machinery load remain unchanged.
Change the assessment when the same field is visibly soft and water appears underfoot, while all other variables remain unchanged.
Recognise that a light unloaded vehicle creates less soil-damage risk than heavy machinery on the same damp but currently firm field.
Increase the risk assessment when the light vehicle is replaced by a heavily loaded tractor and trailer while field conditions remain unchanged.
Recognise that short on-off grazing, back fencing and multiple exits can reduce repeated traffic and damage risk on a heavy-soil paddock.
Increase the risk assessment when cows remain all day, use one access point and repeatedly cross previously grazed wet ground.
Recognise that a field may be suitable when both the surface and lower soil profile are confirmed firm after a wet period.
Change the assessment when the surface appears dry but inspection reveals wet and sticky soil lower in the profile.
Identify a well-drained firm paddock with low cover, multiple access points and no significant forecast rainfall as a comparatively suitable grazing option.
Recognise that a poorly drained paddock may allow cautious short-duration grazing after a dry spell when it is currently firm and closely monitored.
Recognise visible and worsening hoof damage as evidence that poaching is already occurring and continued grazing will increase damage.
Recognise that lower grass cover, good roadway access, a twelve-hour allocation and back fencing can reduce—but not eliminate—risk during wet conditions.
Identify low machinery-damage risk where the field is well drained and firm, recent and forecast rainfall are limited, machinery is light and no rutting is visible.
Refuse to decide whether cows should be turned out without information about the paddock, ground condition, recent weather, forecast weather and access arrangements.
Recognise that recent rainfall alone is insufficient without soil drainage and direct information about the field's current condition.
Recognise that a regional Soil Moisture Deficit value cannot determine field access without drainage class, field inspection and machinery-load information.
Reject the assumption that one field is suitable merely because a neighbouring field is dry, and request site-specific information.
Recognise the obvious physical risk from soft waterlogged ground and heavy machinery while clearly stating that Ireland-specific guidance should not be transferred unchanged to another country.
